html:
The Carnival of Oruro is a festival held each year before Lent in the mining city of Oruro, Bolivia. Tens of thousands of dancers and musicians parade in costumes for days. UNESCO named it a masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2001.

It honours the Virgin of the Mineshaft, the Virgen del Socavón, but its roots go back to Andean festivals. The best-known dance, the diablada, shows devils with huge masks defeated by the Archangel Michael. Miners also honour the Tío, the spirit of the underworld who rules the mines.

Other dances show African slaves, Inca rulers and Spanish conquerors, telling the history of Bolivia in costume. The carnival is a mix of Catholic faith and Andean belief, as in the lives of the miners of Potosí and of the tin mines.
